chapter_theme: Marutham, the close of the book (140-153) and its preface: the husband's straying and the wife's sulk, told through the field buffalo raiding the pond, the bard turned away, the son carried home as a passport, and the eyes that never see him in any phase of the quarrel.

140.reading: The bee that will not drink even in the lotus flower, holding that the honey laid up inside the earth-rooted banana cluster is its own, has its likeness in the lord of the eye-filling field town, and the daughter of that bewitched town, knowing his nature, strings her garland to suit it.
140.nuance: A hidden comparison is near: the bee that scorns the lotus for honey it calls its own is like the lord who leaves the wife for another house. It is left untagged because the pairs cannot be fixed on this text: who 'strings' (தொடுப்பாள்) and what, and who the 'daughter of the bewitched town' is, turn on a broken last line. தேன் is read as the bee, as often in this book.

thinai_evidence.note: banana, lotus and the field town of the marutham lord

141.reading: When he said he had sported in the water with fair women of lovely voice, the lady with a voice like a bell sulked; such is the town of fields fed by running water where the blue kingfisher sits and wearies by the path.
141.nuance: He reports the sulk with his own boast in it (ஆடினேன், 'I sported'), so the offence and the account of it come from one mouth. The two voices are matched, அணிக்குரல் for the other women and மணிக்குரல் for the wife.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk over his water-play with other women

comparisons.tenor: the wife's voice, clear as a bell

142.reading: The friend tells the lord of the field town, where in the cool pond the stooping hen keeps to her tall cock among the lotus, that his chest is like a rich pool, and that the wife, with a single craving like a pregnant woman's for sour things, wants it as the only cure for the longing that will not leave her.
142.nuance: The hen keeping to her mate could be read as iraicchi (as she clings, so the wife wants only him), and the deletion test would pass; it is left as scene because the verb of line 2 (புண்கயத்துள்ளும்) is doubtful, so the act cannot be fixed. The pond of line 1 returns in line 2 as the simile for his chest (வண்கயம்), so the scene and the comparison share one word.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus pond of the field town

comparisons.tenor: his chest, cool and refreshing as a rich pool
her single longing for him, as fixed as a pregnant woman's craving for sour food
his chest as the medicine for her love-sickness

143.reading: No sooner had she embraced the sandal-smeared chest of the lord of the good field town, before she had even turned on her side, than the cock that lives at the foot of the poor folk's huts woke the sleepers and the dawn tune began to hum.
143.nuance: The night is measured in a single gesture: புடைபெயரா மாத்திரைக்கண், 'in the time it takes not even to turn aside'. That the cock lives among the huts of the poor (புல்லியார் கூட்டு) sets the lovers' brief night against the town's working day that the bird begins.

thinai_evidence.note: the field town at cock-crow, marutham's dawn

144.reading: The courtesan, wrapped in red cloth, smeared with paste that yellows her jewels and wearing red water-lilies with care, sends him off towards his house in style, coaching him: 'even if she looks at you and speaks, do not answer'.
144.nuance: Read with பரத்தை as the subject of all three participles and of விடும், the verse turns the wife's complaint into a report of the rival's stage-management: she dresses him off, even scripts his silence. Read otherwise (the warning as the wife's), the sense changes, so the verse is marked uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan sends the husband home to face his wife

145.reading: With the noise of songs, of tunes and of the unbending horns all crowding together, rising like a hooded serpent that rears at a charm, he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
145.nuance: கோட்டரவம் is used twice with two senses: in line 2 the sound of horns (கோடு, horn), in line 3 the serpent with a curved hood. Indra is marutham's god (porul 1.5), so the simile places the husband's return in his own landscape. The pomp may be mocking: he needs a procession and a child to get through the door.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband comes back bringing his son, under marutham's god

comparisons.tenor: the husband arriving with his son amid music
his proud bearing as he enters

146.reading: Though the great of this earth-bound world went on slighting her for days past counting, she of the pearl-strung breasts, letting go the reserve that is a woman's nature, made herself wholly gentle.
146.nuance: The verse repeats கிடந்த three times (மண்கிடந்த, எண்கிடந்த, பெண்கிடந்த): the earth that lies there, the days that lie uncounted, the nature that lies in a woman, and only the last is undone.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing; the colophon's marutham and the sulk given up decide it

147.reading: The red-eyed, black-horned buffalo, with a little lowing, plunges into the field pond of the lovely fields and comes back crowned with blue lilies and red kayal fish, carrying frogs on its back as well.
147.nuance: This is the classic marutham ullurai vehicle (the buffalo that raids the pond and comes home wearing its flowers, as the husband comes home with other women's marks), but nothing in the verse or its colophon states the situation, so condition 4 fails and the buffalo is scene. The frog riding home on its back is a comic touch no Sangam buffalo has.

thinai_evidence.note: the field buffalo in the lily pond

comparisons.tenor: the buffalo decked with the pond's spoils like a reveller with a garland

148.reading: The dark-horned buffalo, like darkness walking, having grazed the great field pond where all is confusion, with horns that could shift stones, lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing a cover of paddy straw.
148.nuance: Unlike verse 147, this buffalo's raid ends with a return, and the cause given is the calf (தன் கன்றுள்ளி). Read as iraicchi it would say the husband should come home for his son, but the verse has no other sense to survive the deletion test, so the buffalo is the subject, not a carrier.

thinai_evidence.note: the buffalo, the field pond and the paddy stack

comparisons.tenor: the black buffalo, dark as walking night

149.reading: Even if you leave her and live apart, a woman's nature is something else: see how she of eyes like red kayal fish, not wasting away, only feels shame, before even a tune has been played.
149.nuance: Line 2 repeats the phrase of verse 146, பெண்கிடந்த தன்மை, and here the woman's nature holds where there it gave way: shame (நாணும்) instead of pining (நையாது).

thinai_evidence.note: only the colophon's marutham places it; the line naming the land is corrupt

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, long and red-edged like the kayal fish

150.reading: O bard of the lute of mingled strings, what of it when one looks closely? Reckoned up, there is none today in the sea-ringed world equal to her; if there were any in the circle of the mighty, so be it.
150.nuance: Turning the bard away by praising the wife's worth rather than blaming the husband leaves the bard nothing to argue with. Line 3's கல் பெயர் சேராள் is obscure in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard as go-between belongs to the marutham quarrel; no native thing of the land

151.reading: The wife tells the bard of the great-stemmed lute that her son, with anklet bells on his mud-splashed feet and a red-gold plate on his brow, plays in the dust before this house and will not play as other women's do; today his father may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
151.nuance: எங்கையர், 'our younger sisters', is the wife's ironic courtesy for her rivals. The verb ஆடு runs through the verse in three senses: the son plays in mud and dust, the other women 'play', and the husband may go and sport.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard and the courtesans of the marutham quarrel; the mud is the only sign of the land

152.reading: The wife tells her husband not to embrace her: the marks printed on his chest by another woman's breasts, jewels and leaf-paintings would be wiped away by their son's wet mouth, and her breast milk would spoil his garland.
152.nuance: The refusal is phrased as care for his finery: what the son's mouth and her milk would 'spoil' is the evidence of the other woman (இட்ட குறி), so her concern is the accusation. உலையாது, 'without fail', makes the spoiling certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife refuses the embrace of a husband marked by another woman

153.reading: Neither in the look of sulk, quarrel and pique she kept up, nor in the love of the ripe union that followed, has she seen him; and if he goes off angry her eyes tremble without shame: her eyes never once see the lord of the dense field town.
153.nuance: The three grades of the quarrel are named in a row (துனி, புலவி, ஊடல்) and then union is called 'ripe' (கனி), the vocabulary the Kural uses in its chapter on புலவி. The paradox is that every stage of the cycle hides him from her eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the cycle of sulk and union with the lord of the field town

payiram.reading: The prefatory verse says that the poet, ripe in the doctrine of secret love, bound the Thinaimalai, a garland of paired landscapes, in matchless sweet Tamil, so that the displeasure of the critical might cease and the book come easily to the hand of those who study it.
payiram.nuance: கணிந்தார் in line 2 seems to play on the poet's name, Kanimethaviyar, and the book is offered as a garland (மாலை) twice over: இணைமாலை and திணைமாலை.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the poet and his book, the nearest puram class to a eulogy

links.note: Ainkurunuru 65: the wife tells the lord not to embrace her body that has borne a son, since it would spoil his chest. Thinaimalai 152: do not embrace me; our son's wet mouth would wipe off the marks of breasts, jewels and leaf-paint on your chest, and my milk would spoil your garland.
links.teaches: The Ainkurunuru's mother refuses the embrace by pretending to protect his chest from her post-partum body; the Thinaimalai keeps that pretext and names what is on the chest, another woman's marks, so the pairing shows the old formula of 'spoiling' was an accusation waiting to be made explicit.

links.note: Akananuru 26: the wife recalls that lately her husband held back from embracing her for fear of spilling the milk meant for their son. Thinaimalai 152: the wife herself refuses his embrace, saying her milk would spoil his garland.
links.teaches: In the Akananuru it is the husband who fears the milk and the wife who is hurt by his caution; in the Thinaimalai the wife takes up the same fear as her weapon, so together they show the nursing mother's milk standing on either side of the quarrel, as his excuse or as her refusal.

links.note: Kural 1311: all women feast on you in common with their eyes, philanderer; I will not come near your chest. Thinaimalai 152: the wife refuses her husband's marked chest under cover of the son's drool and her milk.
links.teaches: The Kural's wife refuses the chest openly and for the least offence, being looked at; the Thinaimalai's wife has proof printed on the chest and still refuses only by indirection, so the couplet's open charge and the quatrain's domestic pretext mark two registers of one refusal, the second keeping the house's peace while making the charge.

links.note: Kural 1306: without துனி and புலவி, love is like over-ripe and unripe fruit. Thinaimalai 153: in துனி, புலவி and ஊடல், and in the கனி union after, her eyes never see the lord.
links.teaches: The Kural justifies the graded quarrel as what keeps love ripe, while the Thinaimalai uses the same three words from inside the cycle and finds that none of its stages, quarrel or ripe union, lets her look at him, so the pair sets the doctrine of the quarrel as seasoning against its cost to the one who lives it.

links.note: Kural 1285: as the eye does not see the brush that lines it, I do not see his fault when I see him. Thinaimalai 153: my eyes never see the lord, in sulk, in union, or when he leaves in anger.
links.teaches: The Kural finds one moment when the eye cannot see, nearness blinding it to his fault; the Thinaimalai extends that blindness to every phase of the marutham quarrel and to the man himself, so the couplet's single paradox becomes a whole cycle in which closeness and distance alike keep him out of view.

links.note: Natrinai 250: the man, come home with his son, tells the bard how his wife, seeing him approach, shrank away like a startled doe asking 'who are you?'. Thinaimalai 145: amid songs, tunes and horns he came carrying his son to our place like Indra.
links.teaches: The Thinaimalai gives the son-bearing return from outside, as a procession fit for Indra, and the Natrinai gives it from the man's side, where the same entry ends in his wife's recoil, so together they show that the son as passport was a public spectacle whose private outcome the poets left open.

links.note: Akananuru 46: the red-eyed buffalo breaks its tether, raids the pond, scatters the fish and eats the lotus, and the friend says he has brought another woman home. Thinaimalai 147: the red-eyed black-horned buffalo plunges into the field pond and comes back crowned with lilies and kayal fish and carrying frogs.
links.teaches: The Akananuru states the situation the raiding buffalo stands for, while the Thinaimalai keeps only the image and adds the buffalo coming home dressed in the pond's spoils, which shows the image had become a sign of the straying husband that a later poet could leave unexplained and even play for comedy.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 95: the black-horned buffalo snaps its rope and grazes the long-eared paddy all morning; its lord gives her pain even by day. Thinaimalai 148: the dark-horned buffalo grazes the great field pond, then lows remembering its calf and comes home wearing paddy straw.
links.teaches: The Ainkurunuru's straying buffalo is left grazing, as the husband is left away, while the Thinaimalai brings the same animal home and gives the calf as the reason, so the pairing shows the marutham buffalo could carry the wife's hope as well as her complaint: the child that draws the stray back.

links.note: Natrinai 380: the friend refuses the bard, saying they are soiled with ghee and smoke and smell of the new-born son, no match for the decked women of his master's street. Thinaimalai 151: the wife tells the bard her son plays in the dust before this house, not as other women's do, and his master may go and play with 'our younger sisters'.
links.teaches: Both refuse the bard by setting the soiled household against the decked rivals, but the Natrinai turns the grime on the women of the house as mock unfitness, while the Thinaimalai turns it on the son and calls the rivals 'our younger sisters', so the same refusal could be humble or proud depending on whom the dirt is laid on.

source_issues: The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers and addressees are inferred from the verses, with occasion words null.
Verse 140 line 4 'மயல் ஊ ரரவர்' is broken in spacing and probably corrupt (perhaps மயலூரவர்); who 'strings' and what is unclear.
Verse 142 line 2 'புண்கயத் துள்ளும்' is doubtful in sense; a verb of clinging or embracing is expected.
Verse 146 line 3 'மூலையினாள்' looks like a misprint for முலையினாள் (of the breasts).
Verse 149 line 1 'புள்மனுநுன்' is corrupt, and the sense of line 3 'பண்கிடந்து செய்யாத மாத்திரையே' is uncertain.
Verse 150 line 2 has unbalanced editorial brackets ('மற்(று(இன்(று)'), and line 3 'கல் பெயர் சேராள்' is obscure.
Verse 153 line 1 'நோக்கு(எ)ன்' carries an editor's inserted letter; the reading takes it as நோக்கு என்.
